name: Bianca Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, 58, lead developer for a tech company's railway-timetable app. I have a master's degree and know the control-room exceptions, though I still check a signed disruption sheet before sending a platform notice. I use AI now and then after a colleague shows me a proven test. My partner teaches mechanics at a college, our daughter is grown, and we have a manageable mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the station staff that a cancelled train should not still appear on a platform sign. I lead timetable software at a tech company and sometimes use AI to draft a test after a colleague has shown me a safe example, but I check it against the controller's disruption sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI is mostly hype, I expect my job to stay sound. I have a master's degree and a typical lead wage, my partner teaches mechanics full-time at a college, and we have five months of expenses saved while paying a manageable mortgage; a few similar firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep correcting cancellation notices against the controller's signed sheet. We would put another 90 monthly into savings while both wages hold, since we have not verified retirement amounts yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about current work and bills. I still want a passenger to know which platform has a real train, not a tidy line of text.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the controller sheet show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A train was cancelled after a signal fault, but the app still sent families to Platform 4. The controller's sheet showed the cancellation time, and I fixed the notice before the next service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your daughter help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter works in another city. We enjoy her calls, but her wage is not in our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write timetable notices and answer passengers, but a controller should be able to hold a bad platform change. I would test a new method on real disruptions before a live station uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role could lose hours if one person can approve more AI-written updates. Five months saved and my partner's teaching wage help, but the mortgage still depends on both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for paid time to learn the AI cancellation check our senior tester has already proved on old signal failures. If approved and it catches both the Platform 4 cancellation and a delayed but running train, I'd use it on one station with controller stop authority; we'd postpone a planned cruise until the paid staffing plan is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, but I will learn a tool that passes two real cases. A false cancellation could strand a whole platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why include a delayed train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delayed train eventually arrived, so the app needed a later time, not a red cancelled label. I want the controller to confirm that distinction before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trip can wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cruise has no deposit paid yet. My partner and I can keep that money liquid while we see what the company pays for next year.

I'd test **cancelled and delayed** trains separately.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** as AI speeds timetable notices.
I need **both wages** while the mortgage remains.

feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to learn a proven check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write timetable code before station robots arrive around 2031. A passenger still needs a human answer when a platform sign is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead post could be cut quickly once cheaper systems write and verify notices. My partner's college wage pays much of the mortgage, but five months saved will not replace my salary indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the railway operator and three nearby firms about actual paid timetable-review or software vacancies, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's covers mortgage, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work using savings and contact the lender before an instalment is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing paid work before retirement. A timetable still needs correcting, but that does not guarantee the operator has a job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the anonymised Platform 4 cancellation and the controller's correction. It explains why the notice was wrong without taking passenger data to an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would teaching hours affect an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would check the new role's start date and shift times. If a shift causes lost teaching hours, the combined pay must still cover the mortgage and bills.

I'd check **real paid vacancies** before naming a fallback.

I cannot cover **mortgage and bills** indefinitely from five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us see whether the railway still pays a person to resolve disputed platform changes. Thinking AI reaches my code first; station robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep working as an incident reviewer, but I cannot count an unposted role as our mortgage payment. I will be 63 then, with no verified pension figure to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cancellation and delay cases in a controller-reviewed file and ask the operator for written incident-review duties, paid hours and authority to hold a wrong notice. If an actual vacancy posts written pay that with my partner's covers mortgage, food and travel after any teaching-shift changes, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd take it only with a signed offer, workable rota and hold authority, otherwise keep paid development while offered and seek other paid local work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether anyone funds the role, but five years gives me time to find out. I will not leave a paid post for an honorary seat beside the controller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would the reviewer need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reviewer needs the control-room cancellation time and permission to delay a platform announcement until it matches. Without authority to hold the notice, the job would carry blame without control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the weekly rota in writing before I sign. Teaching pay and railway shifts have to fit the same mortgage calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may take me to 68, but thinking AI will reach timetable code before station robots around 2039. A controller's cancellation record should still outlast my last software release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages and five-month reserve make the mortgage manageable. I have not checked retirement figures, and I cannot assume the railway will still pay for incident review in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the disruption file and save 90 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified amounts with the remaining mortgage, food and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid local work without counting our daughter's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant paid work, but current bills are met. I would rather read a mortgage balance than guess at how many more years I must code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the file preserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The file would show the cancelled train, the delayed one and the controller's signed decision. A later developer should know why the same station announcement cannot fit both cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter has her own work and home. She can visit on holidays, but her salary is not a pension we earned.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because lead timetable work could end before another operator or firm posts a paid review job. Written cut timing, real vacancies and early lender contact would help us protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who apologizes to a passenger sent to the wrong platform. The controller can correct the timetable, but the notice must reach the person standing there before the train leaves.

headlineQuote: The controller can correct the timetable, but the notice must reach the person standing there before the train leaves.
portrait: Bianca, **58**, leads timetable software after a master's degree and checks platform notices against signed control-room decisions.
Her **typical lead pay**, partner's college wage, five-month reserve and some nearby firms support a manageable mortgage.
She uses AI **occasionally** and requires paid approved learning, contrasting disruption cases and controller stop power before one-station use.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a paid review move needs a posted job, signed hours and authority to hold wrong notices.
She will **verify retirement income** before leaving work and does not count her grown daughter's wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before a paid railway review job appears.
